resolved_by: Supreme Court in United States v. Taylor, 596 U.S. 845 (2022), which affirmed the Fourth Circuit's Taylor decision and held that attempted Hobbs Act robbery is not a crime of violence under § 924(c) because the attempt must itself involve actual, attempted, or threatened force.
issue: Is an attempt to commit a crime of violence automatically a crime of violence under the § 924(c) force clause, or must the attempt itself involve the attempted, actual, or threatened use of force?

sides.position: An attempt to commit a crime of violence is invariably a crime of violence, because § 924(c) reaches attempted use of force (the pre-Taylor majority rule).
cases: United States v. Walker, 990 F.3d 316 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Smith, 957 F.3d 590 (5th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Ingram, 947 F.3d 1021 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Dominguez, 954 F.3d 1251 (9th Cir. 2020)
United States v. St. Hubert, 909 F.3d 335 (11th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: An attempt is a crime of violence only if the attempt itself involves attempted, actual, or threatened force; an attempt to threaten force is not an attempt to use force.
cases: United States v. Taylor, 979 F.3d 203 (4th Cir. 2020), aff'd, 596 U.S. 845 (2022)
United States v. Richardson, No. 21-4300 (4th Cir. 2024)

this_court: follows the Taylor rule: an attempt is a crime of violence only if the attempt itself involves attempted, actual, or threatened force.
quote: Our decision in Taylor created a split with our sister circuits, and the Supreme Court promptly took up the case.
cite: United States v. Deshaun Richardson, No. 21-4300 (4th Cir. 2024)
